title: MscaleFNO: Multi-scale Fourier neural operator learning for oscillatory functions and wave scattering problems

pages.text:
MscaleFNO: Multi-scale Fourier neural operator learning for 
oscillatory functions and wave scattering problems

a School of Mathematical Sciences, MOE-LSC and CMA-Shanghai, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China
b Department of Mathematics, Southern Methodist University, Dallas, TX, USA

In this paper, a multi-scale Fourier neural operator (MscaleFNO) is proposed to reduce the spectral 
bias of the Fourier neural operator (FNO) in learning high-frequency mapping between highly 
oscillatory functions, with an application to learn the nonlinear mapping between the coefficient 
of the Helmholtz equation and its solution. The MscaleFNO consists of a series of parallel normal 
FNOs with scaled inputs of the function and the spatial variable, and their outputs are shown 
to be able to capture various high-frequency components of the mapping itself and its image. 
Numerical results demonstrate the substantial improvement of the MscaleFNO for the problem 
of wave scattering in the high-frequency regime over the normal FNO with a similar number of 
network parameters.

Partial differential equations (PDEs) play a crucial role in modeling a wide array of natural phenomena and engineering problems, 
such as heat conduction, fluid dynamics, and wave propagation. In recent years, several machine learning approaches have emerged 
for solving PDEs, including Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) [8,22,26] and their recent variants [7], Deep Ritz methods 
[10], Deep Galerkin methods (DGMs) [28], and neural networks based on stochastic differential equations [6,14,23]. PINNs use the 
residual of the PDEs as the loss function, enabling the network to approximate solutions while adhering to the underlying physical 
laws. Deep Ritz methods apply a variational principle by minimizing the associated energy functional. DGMs utilize deep neural 
networks to approximate solutions of PDEs by minimizing residuals at randomly sampled points, eliminating the need for spatial 
meshes and making it suitable for complex domains. SDE-based neural networks incorporate stochastic differential equations into 
neural network frameworks to model dynamic processes and quantify uncertainty. These approaches have shown strong performance, 
especially for high dimensional problems [3,9,33].

Operator learning [1], an alternative way of machine learning to solve PDEs, focuses on learning the mapping between functions 
that represent physical parameters and their corresponding PDE solutions, rather than learning specific solutions for given parameters 
as the methods mentioned above. Unlike the methods that predict outputs based on discrete data points, operator learning aims at 
modeling the relationship between whole functions, making it suitable for tasks like learning PDE-defined operators. This approach 
has been applied to establish cause-effect relations in various systems, such as the material properties of a medium and its scattering 
characteristics in wave scattering, or the seismic excitation and the response of a building. Some well-known operator learning meth-
ods include the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) [17], DeepOnet [5,21], and U-Net [27]. The FNO approximates nonlinear operators

by learning kernel functions directly in the frequency domain via Fourier transforms. The DeepONet, based on the universal approx-
imation theorem for nonlinear operators [5], employs a branch network to encode the input function and trunk network to create a 
basis for the output function space, to approximate the mapping between input and output function spaces. It is similar in some way 
to a generalized discrete Fourier transform but using a learned basis (trained trunknet) where the branchnet acts like generalized 
discrete Fourier coefficients. The U-Net architecture, characterized by its encoder-decoder structure with skip connections, has also 
demonstrated effectiveness in learning complex operator mappings.

Many practical problems involve quantities with significant high-frequency components, which poses a challenge to the deep 
neural network (DNN) learning due to the well-known spectral bias of the DNN learning toward low-frequency content during 
the training [30]. Various approaches have been proposed to remove the spectral bias of the neural networks such as the Multi-
scale DNN (MscaleDNN) [19] and Phase Shift DNN [4], and a more detailed review of different approaches is given in [29]. The 
MscaleDNN and Phase Shift DNN methods aim to improve the network’s ability to capture high-frequency components by using 
frequency transformation techniques of converting higher frequency components into lower ones with scaling or phase shifting, 
respectively. So far, these approaches have been used for the direct learning of the PDE solution. It is our objective in this paper to 
address the spectral bias of operator learning.

Specifically, this paper extends the MscaleDNN approach to the FNO framework, giving a Multi-scale Fourier neural operator 
(MscaleFNO). The MscaleFNO consists of multiple parallel FNOs, each processing scaled inputs of both the function and the inde-
pendent variable of the function, enabling the network to capture a broader range of high-frequency components in the mapping. 
This approach is particularly effective for problems involving highly oscillatory functions, such as the nonlinear mapping between 
the coefficients of the Helmholtz equation and its solution, by reducing the spectral bias and enhancing the accuracy at fine scales. 
It should be mentioned that some existing work on reducing the spectral bias of operator learning includes the hierarchical attention 
neural operator [18]. In [24], a diffusion model is integrated with various neural operators to improve their spectral representation 
of turbulent flows. The MscaleFNO is a novel multi-scale architecture, specifically designed to overcome the spectral bias of the 
FNO. Our results show that MscaleFNO offers improved performance compared to the standard FNO, especially for high-frequency 
components.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents some preliminaries on FNO and their parameter descriptions. The 
MscaleDNN and MscaleFNO will be introduced in Section 3; in addition, the scattering wave mapping from scatter properties will 
be described. Section 4 contains numerical tests for a model nonlinear mapping which mimics the Green’s function of the Helmholtz 
equation, and the Helmholtz solution mapping. Finally, a conclusion is given in Section 5.

The Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) was first proposed by Li et al. [17] as a data-driven model for learning mappings between 
infinite-dimensional spaces from observed input-output data. Unlike other neural operator architectures such as Deep Green networks 
[11] and DeepONet, the FNO relies on the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), efficiently implemented via the Fast Fourier Transform 
(FFT), to evaluate a convolution kernel operator. The O(Nlog N) scaling of FFT significantly speeds up the evaluation of the kernel 
operator, making the FNO particularly efficient for high-dimensional problems. However, this approach limits the domain of the 
mapped functions to rectangular shapes and is most effective for low-dimensional spaces, such as the targeted application of solving 
Helmholtz equations in Rd, where d= 1, 2, 3.

In practical implementation, the output function often contains components that exhibit spatial dependence beyond their direct 
correlation with the input function. This phenomenon is particularly evident in dynamic systems with source terms, where u represents 
the solution and a characterizes the initial or boundary conditions or material parameters. In such cases, the solution u inherently 
incorporates information determined by the spatial distribution of the source terms.

To effectively handle this spatial dependency, the FNO architecture explicitly incorporates both the spatial coordinate x and the 
function values a(x) as input variables. Here, the spatial coordinate x plays a crucial role in capturing the position-dependent feature 
of the solution u(x). Mathematically, we can interpret the coordinate input as an identity mapping of x: idD(x) = x, for x∈D⊂Rd.

The multi-scale DNN(MscaleDNN), proposed in [19] uses a simple parallel architectural framework to approximate functions 
f∶Ω →R with a wide range of spectral content for a general domains Ω ⊂Rd. This architecture is designed to reduce the spectral 
bias of DNNs [25,31]. The spectral bias of DNNs refers to the fact that neural networks exhibit preferential learning of low-frequency 
components over their high-frequency counterparts.

The MscaleDNN employs a collection of sub-networks with different scaled inputs to approximate the target function f(x) at 
different frequency ranges. A key feature of the method lies in its ability to capture features across multiple scales simultaneously 
through its parallel network structure. fθi(αix) denotes an individual neural network with parameters θi operating on scaled input αix, 
where αi represents the scaling factor. A property of this structure is that larger values of αi enable the corresponding sub-network to 
capture and learn higher-frequency components of the target function f(x).

In complex physical systems, high-frequency components play a vital role in determining system dynamics. However, traditional 
neural networks often struggle to capture these features accurately. While MscaleDNN has demonstrated remarkable capability in 
handling multi-scale features for function approximation tasks, the challenges in operator learning are substantially more complex, 
requiring the capture of high-frequency patterns across both spatial dimensions and function spaces.

Inspired by the scaling argument in MscaleDNN, we observe that a scaling transformation applied to the input function can convert 
a high-frequency operator into one dominated by lower frequencies, thereby improving the approximation properties of neural

4.1.  Learning a nonlinear mapping between functions: a(x) to u(x) with u= sin(ma)

u depends solely on the input function a in this case, we only use a as the model input without explicitly incorporating the spatial 
variable x. For simplicity, we set the input spatial variable x= 0 in the model.

We have proposed a multi-scale Fourier neural operator to improve the spectral representation of the neural network in learning 
high-frequency mapping between oscillatory functions, such as the one between material properties of a scatterer and its scattering 
field, especially in high-frequency scattering regime. Numerical experiments have shown that the MscaleFNO significantly outper-

forms the normal Fourier neural operator (FNO), particularly when applied to 1-D and 2-D Helmholtz equations, demonstrating 
strong performance in solving high-frequency nonlinear mappings between oscillatory functions. For future research, the choices of 
scales employed in the MscaleFNO can be optimized in an adaptive and dynamical manner as proposed in [12]. Future work can also 
include applying the MscaleFNO to inverse medium problems in high-frequency wave scattering.
